program.how: written for ounce-core from the algorithm description; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: for the 128-, 192- and 256-bit key the RFC 6114 Appendix A ciphertext matches (3 of 3) and decrypting it returns the plaintext (3 of 3)

Appendix B intermediate values match: L (LL and LR) 20 of 20 words, whitening keys 12 of 12 words, round keys 132 of 132 words (36 + 44 + 52), the state at the start of every round 66 of 66 (18 + 22 + 26)
the 236 key-schedule constants generated by the GF(2^16) recurrence equal Tables 7 to 9 (60 + 84 + 92)

expected_values_source.what: Appendix A and Appendix B of RFC 6114 (M. Katagi and S. Moriai, "The 128-Bit Blockcipher CLEFIA", 2011), plus its Tables 1 and 2 (the S-boxes S0 and S1) and Tables 7 to 9 (constants), all parsed from the RFC text by a script
expected_values_source.note: the algorithm was written from the RFC's specification, not from the FSE 2007 paper (not fetched). Data copied as numbers; no reference code was copied

negative_control: built with CLEFIA_Q16=0x243e (Q(16) one below its value 0x243f), constants match only 118 of 236, round keys 0 of 36 (128-bit), the three ciphertexts differ, 0 of 3 key sizes fully match and the program exits 1
not_checked: security claims, speed or hardware figures
the full-round differences between key sizes beyond these three published vectors
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about the authors' hardware)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, reproduces every intermediate value and the three ciphertexts published in RFC 6114. It does not show CLEFIA is secure.
